title: Salutation to the armed One
hook: namo sastr paane: salutation to the One with weapons in hand, the protector (Jaap)
tomorrow: Sun of suns, moon of moons

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajooni, never born, not made of earth or water, and your line, not made of this. Today Jaap does something surprising: after formless and unborn, it puts a weapon in the One's hand. Day three hundred forty-one.

A lifeguard's whistle. A crossing guard's raised hand and bright vest. A parent stepping, without thinking, between a child and a dog that's barking too hard. Protection doesn't always look gentle. Sometimes it's loud, and fast, and holding something. The lifeguard has a rescue tube. The guard has a stop sign. The people who stand between us and harm are rarely remembered as soft. They're remembered as there. Jaap Sahib has a line for the One who stands there. Today: salutation to the armed One.
screen: `A LIFEGUARD'S WHISTLE.` → `A PARENT STEPS BETWEEN.` → `PROTECTION ISN'T ALWAYS GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Among the salutations comes this one: namo sastr paane. Namo, a bow. Sastr, or shastar, is a weapon held in the hand, like a sword. Paan is the hand. Salutation to the One with weapons in hand. The next words add astr, a weapon that's thrown or shot, like an arrow: the One honored with that weapon too. It can be startling, right after aroop and ajooni, formless and unborn. Why would the formless need a sword? Because for the Tenth Guru, the sword is a picture of protection. He lived in violent years. His father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi. The Guru himself fought battles to defend his people, and in his Persian letter, the Zafarnama, he speaks of the four sons he lost. In that letter he wrote, in effect, that when every other way has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Not first. Last. So in Jaap the weapon in the One's hand isn't a threat to the innocent. It's the arm that defends them. That idea runs right through Sikh life. The Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings, begins by remembering Bhagauti, a name for the Divine as sword and power. Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, a promise to protect, not a tool for picking fights. And the ideal has a name you met last year: sant sipahi, the saint-soldier. Gentle in the heart, ready in the hands. Jaap bows to the One who is both.
screen: `SASTR: A WEAPON HELD IN THE HAND.` · `WHY DOES THE FORMLESS NEED A SWORD?` · `ZAFARNAMA: THE SWORD COMES LAST.` · `SANT SIPAHI: THE SAINT-SOLDIER.` · then, large: `THE PROTECTOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who protects you, or once did. A parent, a friend, a teacher, a nurse, a stranger who stepped in. Picture them clearly: their face, their hands, the moment they stood between you and harm. Breathe in, and remember what that safety was like. Breathe out, and thank them, silently. Then ask, gently: is there someone I stand between and harm? If you pray, you can say namo sastr paane. The bell holds the time.
Shastar. A weapon held in the hand — namo sastr paane, Jaap's bow to the One with weapons in hand, the protector who defends the weak.
Your line: the protector. Today, stand between someone and a small harm: a mean comment, a rushed decision, a forgotten bill. Be there. Day three hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 341 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SUN OF SUNS, MOON OF MOONS.`

fork.setup: you're the Tenth Guru, and every peaceful way of protecting your people has failed. what does the Zafarnama say?
options: it is then right to take up the sword.
fork.reveal: the letter says the sword is lawful only when all other means have failed: the sword comes last.

original.note: Gurmukhi: shastar, a weapon held in the hand; Jaap writes it sastr, in namo sastr paane.

trapdoor: what you thought: the armed One sounds like a warlike God.
what it means: the weapon is a picture of protection, the arm that defends the weak, used last, not first.
what a scholar hears: Jaap pairs sastr (hand-held weapon) and astr (missile); the Zafarnama, addressed to Aurangzeb, frames armed resistance as lawful only after all other means fail.
recall: singing the Guru's hymns in praise of God

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the year 1675 and 'famous'; the four sons are now tied to the Zafarnama's own mention (source added); 'most gatherings' and 'most Sikh gatherings' changed; 'the One who knows every weapon' corrected toward astr maane; the practice no longer tells the listener what to feel
'namo sastr paane, namo astr maane' transliteration and the gloss of 'astr maane' (knower/honorer of missile weapons): confirm.
Zafarnama verse (commonly numbered 22): paraphrased; confirm numbering and wording.
Guru Tegh Bahadur executed in Delhi, 1675; the Guru lost all four sons (two in battle at Chamkaur, two executed at Sirhind): confirm phrasing.
Bhagauti as the Divine as sword/power in the Ardas: confirm the gloss the Keeper prefers.
Sant sipahi assumed to have been met in year one; confirm.
